title: Accounting Fundamentals
summary: Learn the accounting equation, double entry, the trial balance, financial statements, depreciation and basic ratios, with worked examples you can follow with a pencil.
audience: Students, small business owners and anyone starting in finance or accounting

lessons.title: What accounting does and the accounting equation

body.p: Accounting is the system of recording, classifying and summarising the money events of an organisation so that owners, managers, lenders and tax authorities can make decisions. A market trader who writes sales in an exercise book is doing a small version of it. A company with thousands of transactions does the same job with software and rules. The rules matter because different people must be able to read the same figures and reach the same meaning.

Every business holds three kinds of things. Assets are what the business owns or is owed, such as cash, stock, equipment and money customers still owe. Liabilities are what the business owes to others, such as supplier balances and loans. Equity (also called capital) is the owner's share. The equation is Assets = Liabilities + Equity. It must balance after every single transaction, and that fact is the foundation of the whole subject.

Example: Ada starts a tailoring business by putting 500,000 into a business bank account. Assets (cash) are 500,000, liabilities are 0 and equity is 500,000. If she then borrows 100,000 from a cousin, cash rises to 600,000, liabilities become 100,000 and equity stays 500,000. 600,000 = 100,000 + 500,000, so the equation still balances.

body.tip: Use any currency you like when practising. The rules are the same in naira, cedis, shillings, rand, pounds, euros or dollars.

list: Owners want to know if the business made a profit and how much it is worth.
Lenders want to know if loans can be repaid.
Tax authorities want to know the correct tax due.
Managers want to know which products, branches or months perform best.
Suppliers want to know if the business pays on time.

body.p: Double entry means every transaction is recorded twice, once as a debit and once as a credit, for the same amount. This is how the accounting equation stays in balance. Debit and credit are only labels for the left and right sides of an account. They do not mean good or bad, and a debit does not mean money leaving.

list: Assets and expenses increase with a debit and decrease with a credit.
Liabilities, equity and income increase with a credit and decrease with a debit.

body.p: A useful memory aid is DEAD CLIC. Debit for Expenses, Assets and Drawings. Credit for Liabilities, Income and Capital. Drawings means the owner taking money out of the business for personal use.

steps: Owner puts in 500,000 cash. Debit Cash 500,000 (asset up). Credit Capital 500,000 (equity up).
Buys a sewing machine for 200,000 cash. Debit Equipment 200,000 (asset up). Credit Cash 200,000 (asset down).
Buys fabric for 80,000 on credit. Debit Inventory 80,000 (asset up). Credit Trade payables 80,000 (liability up).
Sells clothes for 150,000 cash. Debit Cash 150,000. Credit Sales 150,000 (income up).
Pays shop rent 30,000. Debit Rent expense 30,000. Credit Cash 30,000.
Pays the supplier 40,000. Debit Trade payables 40,000 (liability down). Credit Cash 40,000.

body.p: Check each line: the debit amount always equals the credit amount. If you ever record only one side, the books will not balance and you must find the missing entry.

Transactions are first written in a book of original entry called the journal (or day book), with the date, the accounts affected, the debit, the credit and a short narration. They are then copied into the ledger, which has one account per item such as Cash, Equipment or Sales. Software does this automatically, but you must understand it to check what the software shows.

body.h: Balancing the accounts for Ada's tailoring business

body.p: Using the six transactions from the previous lesson, the Cash account has debits of 500,000 and 150,000, and credits of 200,000, 30,000 and 40,000. Total debits are 650,000 and total credits are 270,000, so the balance is a debit of 380,000. The Trade payables account has a credit of 80,000 and a debit of 40,000, so the balance is a credit of 40,000.

A trial balance lists every ledger balance in two columns to check that total debits equal total credits. For Ada: Cash 380,000 debit; Equipment 200,000 debit; Inventory 80,000 debit; Rent 30,000 debit; Trade payables 40,000 credit; Capital 500,000 credit; Sales 150,000 credit. The debit column totals 690,000 and the credit column totals 690,000. They agree.

body.tip: A balanced trial balance does not prove the books are right. It can hide an entry posted to the wrong account, an entry left out completely, or two errors that cancel each other. It only proves that debits equal credits.

steps: Recheck the addition of both columns.
Find the difference. If it is exactly divisible by 9, two digits may have been swapped (for example 54 written as 45).
If the difference equals one amount, you may have posted that entry on one side only.
Check each ledger balance was carried over correctly.

lessons.title: The income statement and the balance sheet

body.p: The trial balance is turned into two main reports. The income statement (profit and loss account) shows performance over a period such as a month or a year: income minus expenses equals profit or loss. The balance sheet (statement of financial position) shows what the business owns and owes on one date.

body.h: Ada's income statement for the period

body.p: Sales are 150,000. The only expense recorded is rent of 30,000. Profit is 150,000 minus 30,000 = 120,000. In real life the fabric would normally be treated as stock until used, and only the cost of fabric used would be an expense. Here the 80,000 fabric is still unused and stays on the balance sheet as inventory.

body.h: Ada's balance sheet on the same date

list: Liabilities plus equity: 40,000 + 620,000 = 660,000, which equals total assets.

body.p: The profit of 120,000 is added to equity because profit belongs to the owner. This is the link between the two statements: the income statement explains how equity changed.

body.tip: Profit is not the same as cash. Ada's profit is 120,000 but her cash is 380,000 because she also put in capital and bought assets. A business can be profitable and still run out of cash if customers pay late.

body.p: The accruals concept says income and expenses belong to the period in which they happen, not the period in which cash moves. At the end of a period accountants make adjustments so that each period shows the right figures.

An accrued expense is a cost used but not yet paid, such as electricity used in December and billed in January. Record it as an expense in December and a liability. A prepaid expense is paid in advance, such as 12 months of insurance paid in October. Only the part that covers the current period is an expense; the rest is an asset. If 12,000 pays for 12 months starting 1 October and the year ends 31 December, three months have been used. Expense = 12,000 x 3 / 12 = 3,000, and 9,000 stays as a prepayment.

Equipment loses value as it is used. Depreciation spreads the cost over its useful life instead of charging all the cost in the first year. With straight-line depreciation, annual charge = (cost minus expected residual value) divided by years of life. Ada's machine costs 200,000, is expected to be worth 20,000 after 6 years, so the annual charge is (200,000 - 20,000) / 6 = 30,000. After one year the carrying value is 200,000 - 30,000 = 170,000.

If a customer who bought on credit will never pay, the amount owed is written off as an expense (bad debt) and the receivable asset is reduced. Showing money as an asset when it will never arrive would overstate profit.

body.tip: Depreciation does not use cash in the year it is recorded. It is an allocation of a cost already paid.

lessons.title: Reading the numbers: margins, liquidity and ethics

body.p: Figures mean more when compared. A few simple ratios help you read any small business.

Gross profit is sales minus the cost of the goods sold. If sales are 150,000 and the goods sold cost 90,000, gross profit is 60,000 and the gross margin is 60,000 / 150,000 = 40%. If after other expenses the net profit is 30,000, the net margin is 30,000 / 150,000 = 20%. A falling margin means costs are rising faster than prices.

The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Current means due or expected within a year. If Ada has cash 380,000 and inventory 80,000, her current assets are 460,000. Her current liabilities are 40,000. The ratio is 460,000 / 40,000 = 11.5, so she can cover her short-term debts many times over. A ratio below 1 means short-term bills exceed short-term assets and the business may struggle to pay.

list: Keep receipts, invoices and bank statements for every entry.
Never record sales or expenses that did not happen to change the profit.
Keep business money separate from personal money.
Follow the tax and reporting rules of your country, and ask a qualified accountant for your own situation.

body.p: This course gives you the foundation. Professional accounting qualifications cover tax, audit and reporting standards in depth, and the rules differ by country.

Insurance of 12,000 is paid for 12 months starting 1 October. The year ends 31 December. What is the expense for the year?

options: Profit and cash are always the same thing
Customers may pay late and money may be tied up in stock or equipment
Liabilities are not paid in cash
